messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose exactly 1 design.
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 24.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezoelectric energy harvester (current source + $C_p$ + $R_{leak}$).
    *   Goal: Power load $R_L$ from storage capacitor at node `out`.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6).
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6).
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (Ripple).
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (Startup).
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (Settled).

    *   S1: Nominal ($I_p=50\mu\text{A}$, $f=100\text{Hz}$, $R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$).
    *   S2: Heavy load ($R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$).
    *   S3: Strong excitation, light load ($I_p=100\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=2200\text{k}\Omega$).
    *   S4: Weak excitation ($I_p=30\mu\text{A}$, $R_L=1000\text{k}\Omega$).
    *   S5: Low frequency ($f=80\text{Hz}$, $R_L=470\text{k}\Omega$).
    *   S6: Hot, $C_p$ increase ($C_p=30\text{nF}$, $R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$).

    *   FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) failed S2 (too much load), S3 (voltage too high/ripple), S4 (too little current), and S5 (settled stability).
    *   The piezo open-circuit voltage is low ($\sim 3.2\text{V}$). Diode drops ($0.25\text{V} \times 2 = 0.5\text{V}$) are significant.
    *   To improve efficiency and output voltage, synchronous rectification or SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) is typically used.

    *   A standard SSHI circuit uses an inductor and a switch to flip the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks of the voltage waveform. This significantly increases the energy extracted from the piezo.
    *   Circuit structure for SSHI:
        *   Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        *   Rectification: Full bridge or half-bridge.
        *   Inversion: Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo (or in a specific topology) to invert the charge.
    *   Wait, the goal is $v_{out}$ between $1.8\text{V}$ and $3.6\text{V}$. A simple Zener clamp (DZ33) can prevent $v_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$ (actually $3.3\text{V}$), which helps S3.
    *   To solve S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation), we need better energy extraction. SSHI is the way to go.

    *   Let's consider a Parallel-SSHI or a similar structure.
    *   Simple SSHI:
        *   Piezo (`pzp`, `pzn`).
        *   Rectifier: Diode bridge.
        *   Inversion: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ connected across the piezo terminals.
        *   But wait, the standard SSHI flips the voltage across $C_p$. The simplest implementation is to connect an $L-S$ branch in parallel with the piezo.
    *   Refined SSHI Topology:
        *   Bridge: $D_1(\text{pzp}, \text{out})$, $D_2(\text{pzn}, \text{out})$, $D_3(0, \text{pzp})$, $D_4(0, \text{pzn})$... No, wait, the bridge is $D_1(\text{pzp}, \text{out})$, $D_2(\text{pzn}, \text{out})$, $D_3(\text{out}, \text{pzp})$, $D_4(\text{out}, \text{pzn})$? No.
        *   Standard Bridge:
            $D_1: \text{pzp} \to \text{out}$
            $D_2: \text{pzn} \to \text{out}$
            $D_3: 0 \to \text{pzp}$ (Wait, the prompt says: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]"). Let's follow that.
            $D_1(\text{pzp, out})$, $D_2(\text{pzn, out})$, $D_3(0, \text{pzp})$, $D_4(0, \text{pzn})$.
        *   Now, to invert the charge: An inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
            $L$: `pzp` to `n1`.
            $S$: `n1` to `pzn`.
            $G1$: `SYNC` controller.
            Wait, if $S$ is in parallel with the piezo, it'll short the rectifier. The inversion should happen at the peaks.
            Standard SSHI: the $L-S$ branch is often in parallel with the piezo. The rectifier is then connected to the piezo.
        *   Wait, if I use the provided "full bridge" structure:
            $D_1: \text{pzp} \to \text{out}$
            $D_2: \text{pzn} \to \text{out}$
            $D_3: 0 \to \text{pzp}$
            $D_4: 0 \to \text{pzn}$
            If I put $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo (`pzp` and `pzn`), during the $t_{on}$ time, the inductor will resonate with $C_p$ and flip the voltage.

    *   Let's try a simpler approach: a "half-bridge" (single diode) or a "charge pump" might be too weak. Let's stick to the full bridge with an SSHI-like inversion.
    *   Actually, the most efficient way to implement SSHI is to place the inductor and switch in parallel with the piezo.
    *   Wait, if the inductor is in parallel with the piezo and the rectifier is also in parallel, the inductor will discharge the storage capacitor through the diodes during the flip.
    *   Let's reconsider the components: $L$, $S$, $SYNC$, $D$, $C$.
    *   A better SSHI structure:
        Piezo: `pzp`, `pzn`.
        Rectifier: Full Bridge (as defined).
        $C_{out}$: `out` to $0$.
        Inversion: $L$ and $S$ across the piezo.
        $L$: `pzp` to `n1`.
        $S$: `n1` to `pzn`.
        $G1$: SYNC.
        This flips the voltage $V_{pzp} - V_{pzn}$.
        To avoid S3 (overvoltage), add a Zener clamp: $D_z(0, \text{out})$ with model `DZ33`.

    *   $L \approx \pi^2 f^2 C_p \cdot \dots$ no, the prompt says $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    *   For $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ and $t_{on} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$, $L \approx (t_{on}/\pi)^2 / C_p \approx (1.6\text{e-5})^2 / 25\text{e-9} \approx 10\text{mH}$. (Max $L$ is $10\text{mH}$).
    *   $C_{out}$ should be large enough to minimize ripple: $2.2\mu\text{F}$ to $10\mu\text{F}$.

    *   $D_1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
    *   $D_2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (DSCH)
    *   $D_3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp` (DSCH)
    *   $D_4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn` (DSCH)
    *   $D_z$: `0` $\to$ `out` (DZ33)
    *   $L_1$: `pzp` $\to$ `n1` (10mH)
    *   $S_1$: `n1` $\to$ `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
    *   $G_1$: SYNC (ton=50us, phase=0, edges="both")
    *   $C_1$: `out` $\to$ `0` (4.7uF)

    Wait, if $D_3$ and $D_4$ are as described (anode on ground), $D_3$ is `0` $\to$ `pzp` and $D_4$ is `0` $\to$ `pzn`. This is a standard full-bridge rectifier.
    Wait, the inversion switch $S_1$ closes at the peaks. At the peak, $V_{pzp}$ is max. Closing $S_1$ creates an LC circuit with $C_p$ and $L_1$, which flips the voltage.

    Check the "full bridge" diodes again:
    `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`
    $D_1: \text{pzp} \to \text{out}$
    $D_2: \text{pzn} \to \text{out}$
    $D_3: 0 \to \text{pzp}$
    $D_4: 0 \to \text{pzn}$
    This means:
    - When $\text{pzp} > \text{out}$, $D_1$ conducts.
    - When $\text{pzn} > \text{out}$, $D_2$ conducts.
    - When $\text{pzp} < 0$, $D_3$ conducts.
    - When $\text{pzn} < 0$, $D_4$ conducts.
    This is a full-bridge rectifier.

    Now, the $L-S$ inversion:
    $L_1$ from `pzp` to `n1`.
    $S_1$ from `n1` to `pzn`.
    When $S_1$ closes, we have a loop: `pzp` $\to$ `L1` $\to$ `n1` $\to$ `S1` $\to$ `pzn` $\to$ `Cp` $\to$ `pzp`.
    This will invert the voltage across $C_p$.

    Wait, let's think about $V_{out}$ max. S3 has $I_p = 100\mu\text{A}$ and $R_L = 2.2\text{M}\Omega$. The storage capacitor will charge up. A Zener clamp `DZ33` (anode `0`, cathode `out`) will clamp it at $3.3\text{V}$.

    $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    If $L = 10\text{mH}$ and $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 3.14 \times 5 \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.5\text{ms}$.
    Wait, $t_{on}$ max is $0.001\text{s}$ ($1\text{ms}$).
    Let's try $L = 4.7\text{mH}$. $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{4.7 \times 25 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 3.14 \times 3.4 \times 10^{-4} \approx 1.0\text{ms}$.
    Let's use $L = 1\text{mH}$ and $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{25 \times 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \times 1.58 \times 10^{-4} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
    Actually, the evolution strategy will optimize $L$ and $t_{on}$, so I just need to provide a reasonable starting point.

    Components:
    - $D_1$: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
    - $D_2$: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
    - $D_3$: `0`, `pzp` (DSCH)
    - $D_4$: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
    - $D_z$: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
    - $L_1$: `pzp`, `n1` (1mH)
    - $S_1$: `n1`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
    - $G_1$: SYNC (ton=1e-4, phase=0, edges="both")
    - $C_1$: `out`, `0` (10uF) - max allowed $4.7\text{e-5}$ (Wait, $47\mu\text{F}$? No, $4.7\text{e-5}$ is $47\mu\text{F}$. Let's use $10\mu\text{F} = 1\text{e-5}$).

    Wait, let me double-check the component limits:
    - $C$: $1\text{e-10}$ to $4.7\text{e-5}\text{F}$.
    - $L$: $1\text{e-5}$ to $0.01\text{H}$.
    - $S$: max 4.
    - SYNC: max 2.
    - Components: max 16.

    Let's refine the values:
    - $C_1 = 22\mu\text{F} = 2.2\text{e-5}\text{F}$ (to keep ripple low).
    - $L_1 = 10\text{mH} = 0.01\text{H}$.
    - $t_{on} = 1\text{ms} = 0.001\text{s}$ (max).
    Actually, for $L=10\text{mH}$, $t_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{e-3} \times 25\text{e-9}} \approx 1.57\text{ms}$. Since $t_{on}$ max is $1\text{ms}$, let's use $L=4.7\text{mH}$ and $t_{on}=0.001\text{s}$.

    Is the Zener clamp necessary? S3 is "strong excitation, light load". The reference FBR had $v_{max} = 5.72\text{V}$, which fails $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$. A Zener $D_z$ at $3.3\text{V}$ is definitely needed.

    Will $L-S$ inversion improve S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation)? Yes, SSHI is designed to increase the extracted power from a piezo transducer by flipping the voltage and reducing the time the piezo spends in the "saturated" (non-charging) region of the rectifier.

    - $D_1(\text{pzp, out})$, $D_2(\text{pzn, out})$, $D_3(0, \text{pzp})$, $D_4(0, \text{pzn})$: Full bridge.
    - $C_1(\text{out, 0})$: Storage.
    - $D_z(0, \text{out})$: Clamp.
    - $L_1(\text{pzp, n1})$, $S_1(\text{n1, pzn})$, $G_1(\text{SYNC})$: Inversion.
    Total components: 4 diodes + 1 zener + 1 inductor + 1 switch + 1 sync + 1 capacitor = 9. (Under the 16 limit).

    Wait, let's check the SYNC controller:
    - `edges`: "both" (every half period).
    - `phase`: 0.0 (at the peaks).
    - `ton`: 0.001.

    Wait, one more thing. The piezo model is $I_p \sin(2 \pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$. The voltage peaks when the current is zero. The SYNC controller closes its switches at "the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current." This is exactly what's needed for SSHI.

    One detail: the inductor's series resistance is $2\Omega + 5\Omega/\text{mH}$. For $4.7\text{mH}$, $R_{ser} \approx 2 + 5 \times 4.7 \approx 25.5\Omega$. This is small enough not to kill the efficiency.

    Final check on the bridge:
    - $D_1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
    - $D_2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
    - $D_3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
    - $D_4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
    If $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$, $D_1$ conducts, charging $C_1$.
    If $V_{pzp} < 0$, $D_3$ conducts, completing the circuit to ground.
    This is correct.

    Is there a risk that the inductor current will discharge the storage capacitor?
    When $S_1$ is closed, the path is `out` $\to$ $D_1$ $\to$ `pzp` $\to$ $L_1$ $\to$ `n1` $\to$ $S_1$ $\to$ `pzn` $\to$ $D_4$ $\to$ `0` $\to$ `out`.
    Wait, this path allows the inductor to be charged by the storage capacitor.
    However, the SSHI inversion is meant to be very fast. The energy in $C_p$ is what's primarily being flipped.
    Actually, the most common SSHI circuits avoid this by using a different rectifier or by carefully timing the switch. But given the constraints and components, this is the standard approach.

    Let's double check the "full bridge" description again.
    "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have their anode on ground)"
    Yes:
    $D_1$: pzp $\to$ out
    $D_2$: pzn $\to$ out
    $D_3$: 0 $\to$ pzp
    $D_4$: 0 $\to$ pzn
    This is the exact structure I'm using.
